testName: ICT2613 · May/June 2017 Exam · code practice (verified partial)
sourceType: Paraphrased code practice from the indexed May/June 2017 examination. Only question parts whose wording and expected result are clear in the public preview are included.
sourceLimitations: The source preview is incomplete and some numbering is lost. Unclear or truncated parts are withheld rather than guessed.

questions.text: Write PHP that stores `ICT2613` and `Internet Programming` in two camelCase variables, then uses one echo statement to display `Code: ICT2613, Name: Internet Programming` with the labels Code and Name in bold.
aiRubric: Creates two variables with camelCase names.
Stores ICT2613 and Internet Programming in the correct variables.
Displays both labels in bold using valid HTML.
Produces the requested text in the correct order.
questions.explanation:
PHP variables begin with `$`, and camelCase normally starts with a lowercase word followed by capitalised words, such as `$moduleCode`. HTML tags can be included in the string sent by echo.

Student note: The paper tests several small skills together: variable naming, assignment, string interpolation/concatenation, echo and simple HTML.

questions.text: A POST form contains a text field named `full_name` and three checkboxes named `rone`, `rtwo` and `rthree`. Write PHP that reads the name and stores a clear true/false value for whether each checkbox was selected.
aiRubric: Handles the possibility that full_name is absent.
Checks rone with isset or an equivalent safe existence test.
Stores the results in four variables.
questions.explanation:
Unchecked HTML checkboxes are normally absent from the submitted POST data. Using `isset()` prevents undefined-index warnings and gives a simple boolean result.

Student note: Do not assume every checkbox name will exist in `$_POST`. An unchecked box usually sends nothing.

questions.text: For the older exam style, assume the required module code is already stored in `$moduleCode`. Write one PHP assignment that stores a DELETE SQL statement in `$query` to remove the matching row from table `modules`.
aiRubric: Uses a WHERE condition on the module-code column.
questions.explanation:
The key idea in the exam question is the DELETE statement plus a WHERE clause that limits the row being removed.

Student note: For real applications, use a prepared statement with a bound parameter instead of inserting user-controlled data directly into SQL. The simple string here matches the older paper's learning objective.

questions.text: A program assigns `++` for marks 75 or higher, `+` for 50–74, `*` for 40–49 and `-` below 40. What results are produced for 15, 40, 49, 50 and 78, in that order?
questions.explanation:
15 is below 40, 40 and 49 fall in the 40–49 band, 50 falls in 50–74, and 78 is at least 75.

Student note: Check boundary values carefully. Numbers like 40, 49, 50 and 75 are often used to test whether your conditions overlap or leave gaps.

questions.text:
Rewrite this loop using `do ... while` without changing the output: `$i = 4; while ($i <= 7) { if ($i % 2 != 0) echo "$i - Odd number
"; else echo "$i - Even number
"; $i++; }`
questions.explanation:
A `do ... while` loop executes the body first and checks the condition afterward. Because `$i` starts at 4 and the original while loop also runs immediately, the two versions can produce the same sequence.

Student note: When converting loops, preserve three things: initial value, condition and update step.

`ICT2613` contains seven characters: I, C, T, 2, 6, 1 and 3.

Student note: `strlen()` counts characters/bytes in this simple ASCII string; it does not interpret the digits as one number.

A negative start position counts from the end. Starting two characters from the end of `ICT2613` gives `13`.

Student note: With `substr`, a negative start is measured backward from the end of the string.
